While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Meteorologists have long used the Campbell-Stokes recorder to measure daily hours of bright sunshine.
• Its principal component, a solid glass sphere, functions as a lens, concentrating sunlight onto a treated card set behind it.
• The concentrated rays scorch a thin line into the card.
• As the Sun moves across the sky, the focal point gradually shifts, lengthening the scorched line.
• Passing clouds interrupt the scorching; observers measure the line’s total length to calculate sunshine duration.
items.stem: The student wants to explain how the Campbell-Stokes recorder measures hours of sunshine. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Used by meteorologists to measure daily hours of bright sunshine, the Campbell-Stokes recorder consists of a solid glass sphere that functions as a lens and a treated card mounted behind it.
By concentrating sunlight onto a treated card, the recorder’s glass sphere scorches a line whose darkness indicates how many hours of bright sunshine a location received.
The recorder’s glass sphere focuses sunlight onto a card, scorching a line that grows as the Sun moves and breaks when clouds pass; the line’s length shows how long the Sun shone.
Because the focal point of the recorder’s glass sphere shifts as the Sun moves, the scorched line on the card grows all day, so its length shows the hours since sunrise.
items.explanation: The goal is to explain how the recorder measures hours of sunshine. The notes give a chain: the sphere “functions as a lens, concentrating sunlight onto a treated card,” the rays “scorch a thin line,” the focal point shifts “As the Sun moves across the sky,” “lengthening the scorched line,” and “Passing clouds interrupt the scorching,” so observers “measure the line’s total length to calculate sunshine duration.” Choice C follows that whole chain from the focused sunlight to the measured length.

A.recipe: OG (what the device is, not how it works)
A.why_wrong: It names the recorder’s purpose and parts but never explains how they produce a measurement of sunshine hours.

B.why_wrong: It explains a mechanism, but the notes say observers measure the line’s “total length,” not its darkness.

D.recipe: FALSE (goal-shaped: true first link, cloud link dropped)
D.why_wrong: Its first part is accurate, but the notes say “Passing clouds interrupt the scorching,” so the line does not grow all day, and its length gives sunshine duration, not the hours since sunrise.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (the Campbell-Stokes sunshine recorder, a real meteorological instrument; no figures, no named people beyond the instrument’s name). Band 7 moves: how-goal over a four-bullet chain (focus, scorch, Sun moves, clouds break the line); two goal-shaped FALSE options (B swaps length for darkness, D reverses the cloud link) and one OG description, as in ee51ad04.

fixes: rebuilt D: the old D (scorching only while clouds block the Sun) died on common sense; the new D keeps a true first link and drops the cloud link (hours since sunrise)
paraphrased key C off the notes (“shows how long the Sun shone”)
plainer bullets (mounted to set, narrow line into the card’s surface to thin line into the card); explanation quotes updated

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Sunlit winter bark on fruit trees can warm considerably above the air temperature, then freeze fast at sunset.
• This repeated cycle can split the bark, damage known as sunscald.
• Researchers investigated whether painting trunks with diluted white latex, a traditional orchard practice, prevents sunscald.
• They painted the lower trunks of 40 apple trees, left 40 neighbors unpainted, and put temperature sensors under each tree’s bark.
• Painted trunks stayed up to 9°C cooler on sunny afternoons and split one-third as often.
items.stem: The student wants to present the aim and methodology of the study. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: To test whether painting trunks with diluted white latex prevents sunscald, researchers painted 40 apple trees’ lower trunks, left 40 unpainted, and placed sensors beneath the bark.
Researchers painted the lower trunks of 40 apple trees with diluted white latex and inserted temperature sensors beneath the bark of these trees and of 40 unpainted neighbors.
Seeking to learn whether painting trunks with diluted white latex prevents sunscald, researchers found that painted trunks split only one-third as frequently as unpainted trunks did.
Because sunscald results when sunlit bark freezes fast at sunset, painted trunks, which remained up to 9°C cooler on sunny afternoons, split one-third as frequently as unpainted ones.
items.explanation: The goal has two parts: the study’s aim and its methodology. The researchers “investigated whether painting trunks with diluted white latex ... prevents sunscald,” and to find out, “They painted the lower trunks of 40 apple trees, left 40 neighbors unpainted, and put temperature sensors under each tree’s bark.” Choice A gives both the aim and the method.

B.why_wrong: It describes what the researchers did but never says what they were trying to find out.

C.recipe: OG (aim plus results instead of method)
C.why_wrong: It gives the aim but follows it with a finding, so it never presents how the study was carried out.

D.why_wrong: It explains what causes sunscald and reports the results; it gives neither the aim nor the method.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (sunscald on fruit trees and the orchard practice of painting trunks white). Unnamed, generic study with invented figures (40 trees, 9°C, one-third as often), per WAVE.md. Band 6 shape (8d1ddd1b, 2.21): two-part aim-and-method goal; distractors are method only, aim plus results, background plus results, all accurate.

fixes: plainer bullets (rapidly to fast, every to each) and D to match; explanation quote updated
review.note: Rhetorical Synthesis: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); named people are real and credited only with their documented work, studies are unnamed and generic, no invented names, no literary text.

band7.why: Planned band 6: aim-and-method goal with three accurate study-slot distractors (method only, aim plus results, background plus results) is the band-6 shape (band7 section 6 check 2); a strong band 6.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Early nineteenth-century voters often announced choices aloud or submitted party-printed ballots, frequently colored so observers could identify each voter’s preference.
• In 1856, the Australian colony of Victoria introduced a secret ballot that was printed by the government, listed all the candidates, and was marked in private.
• Britain adopted a similar system in its Ballot Act of 1872.
• American cities and states began using such ballots in 1888; most remaining states followed during the 1890s.
• The system is still sometimes called the Australian ballot.
items.stem: The student wants to provide a historical overview of the secret ballot. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: In 1856, the Australian colony of Victoria introduced a secret ballot, which Britain and most US states then adopted within the next two decades.
First adopted under Britain’s Ballot Act of 1872, the secret ballot spread from there to the colony of Victoria and, beginning in 1888, to American cities and states.
The secret ballot, also called the Australian ballot, lists every candidate and is marked privately, unlike the colored ballots that political parties once printed.
Introduced in Victoria in 1856, the secret ballot reached Britain in 1872 and American cities and states in 1888, replacing spoken votes and party-printed ballots.
items.explanation: The goal is a historical overview of the secret ballot, so the sentence must trace it over time. Choice D starts with Victoria, which “introduced a secret ballot” in 1856, follows it to Britain’s “Ballot Act of 1872” and to the United States, where “American cities and states began using such ballots in 1888,” and notes what it replaced: choices “announced ... aloud” and “party-printed ballots.”

A.why_wrong: It opens accurately, but American cities and states only “began using such ballots in 1888,” more than thirty years after 1856, and most states followed in the 1890s, so the system did not spread to most US states within two decades.

B.why_wrong: It traces a history, but the wrong one: Victoria introduced the secret ballot in 1856, sixteen years before Britain’s Ballot Act of 1872, so the system did not spread from Britain to Victoria.

C.why_wrong: It explains what a secret ballot is and how it differs from party ballots, but it gives no history of when and where it was adopted.

items.notes: Subject: history and social science (the secret ballot: Victoria 1856, UK Ballot Act 1872, US cities and states from 1888, most by the 1890s). Standard dates, no other figures. Band 7 move (section 5, OVERVIEW): band-6 arc kept (PART origin only, OG definition) plus a goal-shaped FALSE option (B tells the history in reverse order). The key does not depend on knowing the term Australian ballot.

fixes: A turned from origin-only PART into a goal-shaped FALSE overview (most US states within two decades)
B rewritten so the reversed order (Britain before Victoria) must be checked against two bullets
key D made exact on the US (“most US states during the 1890s” stretched “most remaining states”); explanation and why_wrong updated
plainer bullets (every candidate to all the candidates, through to in)
review.note: Rhetorical Synthesis: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); named people are real and credited only with their documented work, studies are unnamed and generic, no invented names, no literary text.

band7.why: Historical overview as in 964c6055 with two goal-shaped FALSE overviews (A misreads the timing, B reverses Victoria and Britain) and one OG definition; the key spans origin, spread and what the system replaced, a derived relation.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Hoodoos are slender rock spires that develop as precipitation and repeated freezing gradually erode soft sedimentary layers.
• Some are topped by an erosion-resistant block, called a caprock, that shields the underlying softer rock.
• Geologists compared photographs of three hoodoos in a western US canyon taken three decades apart.
• Hoodoo 1, measuring 14 meters, has a caprock and lost 4 centimeters (cm) of height.
• Hoodoo 2, measuring 9 meters, lacks a caprock and lost 52 cm.
• Hoodoo 3, measuring 8 meters, has a caprock and lost 6 cm.
items.stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of a similarity between two of the hoodoos. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Hoodoos 1 and 3, both more than 10 meters tall, lost less height than the shorter Hoodoo 2, suggesting that taller hoodoos erode more slowly.
Shielded by their caprocks, Hoodoos 1 and 3 each lost only a few centimeters of height in three decades, far less than the uncapped Hoodoo 2.
Hoodoos 1 and 2 each lost less than 10 cm of height over three decades, indicating that both were shielded from erosion by their caprocks.
Like Hoodoo 1, Hoodoo 3 lost some of its height during the three decades between the two sets of photographs.
items.explanation: The goal asks for the significance of a similarity, not just the similarity. Hoodoos 1 and 3 both have a caprock, which “shields the underlying softer rock,” and they lost only 4 and 6 cm, while Hoodoo 2, which “lacks a caprock,” lost 52 cm. Choice B links the shared caprock to the much smaller loss of height.

A.why_wrong: It offers a significance, but Hoodoo 3 measures 8 meters, less than Hoodoo 2, so the two are not both more than 10 meters tall, and the notes credit the caprock, not height.

C.why_wrong: Hoodoo 2 lost 52 cm, not less than 10 cm, and it “lacks a caprock.”

D.why_wrong: It is accurate, but all three hoodoos lost height, so the similarity it names has no significance and it ignores the caprocks.

items.notes: Subject: natural science (hoodoo erosion and caprocks). Unnamed, generic photo survey with invented figures, per WAVE.md. Band 7 moves (section 5, SIM): goal asks for the significance of a similarity; the key derives it from the caprock bullet and the three loss figures; two FALSE options carry the numbers (A misreads Hoodoo 3’s height and credits height, C pairs the wrong hoodoos), one true but trivial similarity. Heights deliberately do not track erosion, so the height reading fails on the numbers.

review.note: Rhetorical Synthesis: no fact-checking (WAVE.md); named people are real and credited only with their documented work, studies are unnamed and generic, no invented names, no literary text.

band7.why: Significance-of-a-similarity goal as in 19b08ead; the key derives the caprock's effect from the shield bullet and three figures; A and C are goal-shaped FALSE options with misread numbers, D a true similarity without significance; heights do not track erosion, so the height reading fails.

While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• Spolia (Latin for “spoils”) are columns, carved stones, or other architectural elements taken from older structures and reused in new buildings.
• Rome’s Arch of Constantine, completed in 315 CE, commemorates the emperor Constantine.
• Several of its sculpted reliefs were taken from earlier monuments honoring the emperors Trajan, Hadrian, and Marcus Aurelius.
• Tunisia’s Great Mosque of Kairouan was extensively rebuilt in the 830s.
• Many marble columns supporting its prayer hall originated in Roman and Byzantine buildings at sites such as Carthage.
items.stem: The student wants to use one of the structures to illustrate the use of spolia. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
options: Completed in 315 CE, Rome’s Arch of Constantine commemorates the emperor Constantine and is decorated with sculpted reliefs.
The Arch of Constantine illustrates the use of spolia, since several of its sculpted reliefs were taken from Roman and Byzantine buildings at sites such as Carthage.
In the Great Mosque of Kairouan, many of the marble columns supporting the prayer hall are spolia, taken from older Roman and Byzantine buildings and reused.
The Great Mosque of Kairouan illustrates the use of spolia, since many of its marble columns were later removed and reused in buildings at Carthage.
items.explanation: To illustrate spolia, the sentence must show one structure built with “architectural elements taken from older structures and reused in new buildings.” Choice C does this with the Great Mosque of Kairouan, whose “marble columns supporting its prayer hall originated in Roman and Byzantine buildings at sites such as Carthage.”

A.why_wrong: It describes the Arch of Constantine but never says that its reliefs came from older monuments, so it does not illustrate spolia.

B.why_wrong: The arch’s reliefs came from “earlier monuments honoring the emperors Trajan, Hadrian, and Marcus Aurelius”; the Roman and Byzantine buildings at Carthage supplied the mosque’s columns.

D.why_wrong: The notes say the columns came from buildings at Carthage and were reused in the mosque, not that they were taken from the mosque and reused elsewhere.

items.notes: Subject: arts and architecture history (spolia: the Arch of Constantine, 315 CE, with Trajanic, Hadrianic and Aurelian reliefs; the Great Mosque of Kairouan, rebuilt in 836, with reused Roman and Byzantine columns). Well-known art history, no figures. • Etching and mezzotint are two techniques for producing prints from metal plates.
• In etching, acid eats lines drawn through a waxy coating into the plate.
• Darker areas of an etching are built up from closely spaced lines.
• Ludwig von Siegen developed mezzotint in the 1640s.
• A mezzotint artist first roughens the whole plate to print solid black, then smooths areas to create lighter tones.

Whereas an etcher builds dark areas from closely spaced lines, a mezzotint artist starts with a plate that prints solid black and works toward light.
In mezzotint, a technique developed in the 1640s by Ludwig von Siegen, an artist roughens the whole plate and then smooths some areas to create lighter tones.
Etching and mezzotint are different techniques, and each gives an artist a distinct way of working on a metal plate.
items.explanation: The goal is to emphasize a difference between the two techniques. Choice B contrasts them with “Whereas”: in etching, “Darker areas ... are built up from closely spaced lines,” but a mezzotint artist “first roughens the whole plate to print solid black, then smooths areas to create lighter tones.”

Both maple seeds and dandelion seeds are dispersed by wind, which carries them away from the parent plant.

• Covered bridges were common in the United States during the 1800s, when many bridges were built of wood.
• A covered bridge’s walls and roof enclose its truss, the framework of wooden beams supporting it.
